vocabulary.definition: Listing what divides a number evenly (its factors) and what it divides into evenly (its multiples), then finding what two numbers share.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Listar lo que divide un número exactamente (sus factores) y lo que el número forma al contar de esa cantidad (sus múltiplos), y luego hallar lo que dos números comparten.
vocabulary.visual: GCF of 48 and 36 is 12 · LCM of 6 and 8 is 24
vocabulary.cloze: Factors ___ a number; multiples are what it ___.

vocabulary.definition: A whole number that divides another number evenly, with no remainder.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un número entero que divide a otro exactamente, sin residuo.

examples.why: It divides with nothing left over.
A factor is never larger than its number.

vocabulary.cloze: A number that divides another exactly, with no remainder, is a ___.

vocabulary.definition: The result of multiplying a number by 1, 2, 3, and so on — where you land when you skip-count by it.
vocabulary.definitionEs: El resultado de multiplicar un número por 1, 2, 3, y así sucesivamente: donde caes al contar de esa cantidad.
vocabulary.cloze: What you land on counting by a number are its ___.

vocabulary.definition: The largest number that is a factor of two or more numbers. It answers “how many equal groups can I make?”
vocabulary.definitionEs: El número más grande que es factor de dos o más números. Responde “¿cuántos grupos iguales puedo formar?”
vocabulary.cloze: The largest number that divides both is their ___ ___ ___.

vocabulary.definition: The smallest number that is a multiple of two or more numbers. It answers “when will these line up again?”
vocabulary.definitionEs: El número más pequeño que es múltiplo de dos o más números. Responde “¿cuándo volverán a coincidir?”
vocabulary.cloze: The smallest number both numbers reach is their ___ ___ ___.

vocabulary.definition: Two factors that multiply to make a number. In a word problem, one is the number of groups and the other is the size of each group.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Dos factores que se multiplican para formar un número. En un problema, uno es la cantidad de grupos y el otro el tamaño de cada grupo.
vocabulary.cloze: Two factors that multiply to make the number are a ___ ___.

vocabulary.definition: Writing a number as a product of prime numbers, usually with a factor tree. Multiplying the primes two numbers share also gives the GCF.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Escribir un número como producto de números primos, normalmente con un árbol de factores. Multiplicar los primos que dos números comparten también da el MCD.
vocabulary.cloze: Writing a number as ___ numbers multiplied together is its prime factorization.

copyPanel.rule: Greatest Common Factor (GCF) & Least Common Multiple (LCM)
steps: 1. GCF: Largest factor shared by two numbers — used to simplify fractions or divide into equal groups
2. LCM: Smallest shared multiple — used to find common denominators
3. Use prime factor trees or list method to find common factors/multiples

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Party Plans
revealWordProblem.text: Reginald is having hot dogs at his party, and 24 people are coming. His mom wants the same number of hot dogs and buns, with none left over. Hot dogs come in packs of 10 and buns come in packs of 8. How many packs of each should they buy, and how many hot dogs and buns will they have?
revealWordProblem.imageAlt: A pack of hot dogs labeled 10 count beside a pack of hot dog buns labeled 8 count.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: Nothing is being split into groups here — packs are being counted forward until the two totals match — so this is a least-common-multiple problem. Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30, 40 …. Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40 …. The first total both pack sizes reach exactly is 40, so the LCM of 10 and 8 is 40. That means 4 packs of hot dogs (4 × 10 = 40) and 5 packs of buns (5 × 8 = 40), giving 40 of each with none left over — more than enough for 24 guests. Any smaller number of packs would leave some hot dogs without buns.

questions.stem: Which list shows all the factors of 12?
questions.explanation: A factor divides 12 evenly. Every one of 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12 does, and nothing else does.
choiceFeedback: Those are MULTIPLES of 12 — where you land skip-counting, not what divides it.
1 and 12 are factors, but so are 2, 3, 4, and 6.
This list forgets 1 and 12, which are always factors of 12.
hints: Ask: what divides 12 with nothing left over?
Try each number from 1 up to 12.
Do not forget 1 and the number itself.
questions.stemEs: ¿Cuál lista muestra todos los factores de 12?
questions.explanationEs: Un factor divide a 12 exactamente. Cada uno de 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 y 12 lo hace, y ningún otro.
hintsEs: Pregunta: ¿qué divide a 12 sin que sobre nada?
Prueba cada número del 1 al 12.
No olvides el 1 y el número mismo.

questions.stem: Which list shows the first four multiples of 8?
questions.explanation: Multiples come from multiplying by 1, 2, 3, 4: 8, 16, 24, and 32 — the numbers you say skip-counting by 8.
choiceFeedback: Those are the FACTORS of 8 — what divides it, not what it makes.
That counts up by 1, not by 8.
That counts by 2.
hints: Skip-count by 8 out loud.
Multiples get bigger; factors stay at or below the number.
questions.stemEs: ¿Cuál lista muestra los primeros cuatro múltiplos de 8?
questions.explanationEs: Los múltiplos salen de multiplicar por 1, 2, 3, 4: 8, 16, 24 y 32 — los números que dices al contar de 8 en 8.
hintsEs: Cuenta de 8 en 8 en voz alta.
Los múltiplos crecen; los factores se quedan en el número o por debajo.

questions.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 12 and 18?
questions.explanation: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. They share 1, 2, 3, and 6 — the greatest is 6.
choiceFeedback: 3 is a common factor, but 6 is also common and larger.
36 is a common MULTIPLE, not a factor — a factor cannot be bigger than the numbers.
2 is a common factor, but not the greatest one.
hints: List the factors of each number.
Circle the numbers that appear in both lists.
Pick the largest circled number.
questions.stemEs: ¿Cuál es el máximo común divisor de 12 y 18?
questions.explanationEs: Factores de 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factores de 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Comparten 1, 2, 3 y 6 — el mayor es 6.
hintsEs: Enumera los factores de cada número.
Encierra los números que aparecen en ambas listas.
Escoge el mayor de los números encerrados.

reviewHighlights.rule: Greatest Common Factor (GCF) & Least Common Multiple (LCM)
steps: 1. GCF: Largest factor shared by two numbers — used to simplify fractions or divide into equal groups
2. LCM: Smallest shared multiple — used to find common denominators
3. Use prime factor trees or list method to find common factors/multiples
reviewHighlights.watchOut: A common mistake is reaching for the wrong tool: listing FACTORS for a problem about repeating cycles. Ayasha's classes repeat every 6 and 8 weeks, so the weeks they land on are multiples — answering with the GCF of 2 claims a class that meets every 8 weeks happens in week 2. Use the size of the answer as a check: a GCF is never larger than the smaller number, and an LCM is never smaller than the larger one.

level1.stem: Sort each number by its relationship to 10.
level1.explanation: Factors divide 10 evenly and are never larger than 10. Multiples are what 10 builds and are never smaller than 10. The number 10 is both a factor and a multiple of itself.
hints: Ask: does this number divide 10, or does 10 divide it?
Factors are at or below 10.
Multiples are at or above 10.
level1.stemEs: Clasifica cada número según su relación con 10.
level1.explanationEs: Los factores dividen a 10 exactamente y nunca son mayores que 10. Los múltiplos son lo que 10 construye y nunca son menores que 10. El número 10 es a la vez factor y múltiplo de sí mismo.
hintsEs: Pregunta: ¿este número divide a 10, o 10 lo divide a él?
Los factores son iguales o menores que 10.
Los múltiplos son iguales o mayores que 10.

level1.stem: What is the least common multiple of 4 and 6?
level1.explanation: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12 …; multiples of 6: 6, 12 …. The smallest they share is 12.
choiceFeedback: 24 is a common multiple, but 12 is smaller and also common.
2 is the greatest common FACTOR of 4 and 6, not a multiple.
10 is 4 + 6 — an LCM is not found by adding.
hints: List multiples of each number.
Look for the first number that appears in both lists.
level1.stemEs: ¿Cuál es el mínimo común múltiplo de 4 y 6?
level1.explanationEs: Múltiplos de 4: 4, 8, 12 …; múltiplos de 6: 6, 12 …. El menor que comparten es 12.
hintsEs: Enumera los múltiplos de cada número.
Busca el primer número que aparece en ambas listas.

level2.stem: Using prime factors, 48 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. What is their GCF?
level2.explanation: Take only the primes both numbers have: two 2s and one 3. Multiplying them gives 2 × 2 × 3 = 12, matching the answer from the factor lists.
choiceFeedback: Multiplying every prime from both trees gives a common multiple, not a common factor.
Both numbers have TWO 2s in common, not one — so the 6 is short a factor of 2.
2 is shared, but 48 and 36 each contain two 2s and a 3, so more is shared than that.
hints: Circle the primes that appear in BOTH trees.
48 has four 2s and one 3; 36 has two 2s and two 3s.
Take the smaller count of each shared prime, then multiply.
level2.stemEs: Usando factores primos, 48 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 y 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. ¿Cuál es su MCD?
level2.explanationEs: Toma solo los primos que ambos números tienen: dos 2 y un 3. Al multiplicarlos da 2 × 2 × 3 = 12, igual que la respuesta de las listas de factores.
hintsEs: Encierra los primos que aparecen en AMBOS árboles.
48 tiene cuatro 2 y un 3; 36 tiene dos 2 y dos 3.
Toma la menor cantidad de cada primo compartido y luego multiplica.

level2.stem: Ayasha has painting every 8 weeks and pottery every 6 weeks, both this week. When do they next fall in the same week?
level2.explanation: Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24 …; multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24 …. The first week they share is week 24.
choiceFeedback: 48 IS a common multiple, but the question asks for the first time they meet — 24 comes sooner.
14 is 8 + 6. Adding the cycles does not find when they line up.
2 is the GCF of 6 and 8 — a factor question, not a cycle question.
hints: List the weeks each class lands on.
Find the first week that appears in both lists.
level2.stemEs: Ayasha tiene pintura cada 8 semanas y cerámica cada 6 semanas, ambas esta semana. ¿Cuándo vuelven a caer en la misma semana?
level2.explanationEs: Múltiplos de 8: 8, 16, 24 …; múltiplos de 6: 6, 12, 18, 24 …. La primera semana que comparten es la semana 24.
hintsEs: Enumera las semanas en que cae cada clase.
Halla la primera semana que aparece en ambas listas.

level2.explanation: Splitting an existing amount into equal groups is a factor question; waiting for repeating cycles to line up is a multiple question. The size of the answer is a useful check on which one you used.
hints: Is the problem breaking something apart or counting forward?
Breaking apart → factors.
Counting forward in cycles → multiples.
level2.stemEs: Clasifica cada problema real según la herramienta que lo resuelve.
level2.explanationEs: Repartir una cantidad existente en grupos iguales es una pregunta de factores; esperar a que dos ciclos repetidos coincidan es una pregunta de múltiplos. El tamaño de la respuesta es una buena manera de revisar cuál usaste.
hintsEs: ¿El problema está descomponiendo algo o contando hacia adelante?
Descomponer → factores.
Contar hacia adelante en ciclos → múltiplos.

level2.stem: Is 4 a factor or a multiple of 12?
level2.explanation: 4 divides 12 evenly (12 ÷ 4 = 3), so 4 is a factor of 12. Multiples of 12 start at 12 and grow.
choiceFeedback: Multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36 … — all at least 12.
4 divides 12, but 12 does not divide 4.
4 × 3 = 12, so it is definitely a factor.
hints: Does 4 divide 12 evenly?
Factors are at or below the number.
12 ÷ 4 = 3, no remainder.
level2.stemEs: ¿4 es un factor o un múltiplo de 12?
level2.explanationEs: 4 divide a 12 exactamente (12 ÷ 4 = 3), así que 4 es un factor de 12. Los múltiplos de 12 empiezan en 12 y crecen.
hintsEs: ¿4 divide a 12 exactamente?
Los factores son iguales o menores que el número.
12 ÷ 4 = 3, sin residuo.

level2.stem: What is the GCF of 10 and 15?
level2.explanation: Factors of 10: 1, 2, 5, 10. Factors of 15: 1, 3, 5, 15. They share 1 and 5; the greatest is 5.
choiceFeedback: 1 is common, but 5 is common and larger.
30 is a common multiple, not a factor.
10 does not divide 15 evenly.
hints: List the factors of each.
Which numbers are in both lists?
Take the largest one.
level2.explanationEs: Factores de 10: 1, 2, 5, 10. Factores de 15: 1, 3, 5, 15. Comparten 1 y 5; el mayor es 5.
hintsEs: Enumera los factores de cada uno.
¿Cuáles números están en ambas listas?
Toma el mayor.

level3.stem: Reginald is having hot dogs for 24 guests and wants the same number of hot dogs and buns, with none left over. Hot dogs come in packs of 10 and buns in packs of 8. How many packs of each should he buy, and how many will he have? Explain which tool you used and why.
level3.sampleAnswer: This is a least-common-multiple problem: the pack sizes repeat, and he needs the first count both can reach exactly. Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30, 40 …; multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40 …. The first number in both lists is 40, so the LCM of 10 and 8 is 40. That means 4 packs of hot dogs (4 × 10 = 40) and 5 packs of buns (5 × 8 = 40), giving 40 of each with nothing left over. It is a multiple problem rather than a factor one because nothing is being split into groups — he is counting packs forward until the two totals match. He will have 40 of each for 24 guests, which is more than enough; buying fewer packs would leave hot dogs or buns unmatched.
hints: Is he splitting an amount into groups, or counting packs forward until they match?
List the multiples of 10 and the multiples of 8.
Find the first total that both pack sizes can reach exactly.
level3.stemEs: Reginald va a servir hot dogs para 24 invitados y quiere el mismo número de salchichas y panes, sin que sobre ninguno. Las salchichas vienen en paquetes de 10 y los panes en paquetes de 8. ¿Cuántos paquetes de cada uno debe comprar, y cuántos tendrá? Explica qué herramienta usaste y por qué.
hintsEs: ¿Está repartiendo una cantidad en grupos, o contando paquetes hacia adelante hasta que coincidan?
Enumera los múltiplos de 10 y los múltiplos de 8.
Halla el primer total que los dos tamaños de paquete pueden alcanzar exactamente.

level3.stem: Claim: “The GCF of two numbers is always smaller than both of them.” Always, sometimes, or never true?
choices: Sometimes — it equals the smaller number whenever that number divides the larger one
Always — a common factor has to be smaller than what it divides
Never — the GCF is always one of the two numbers
Sometimes — it depends whether the numbers are even
level3.explanation: The GCF can never be larger than the smaller number. But it can equal it, when the smaller number divides the larger one exactly. Check 6 and 18: 6 divides 18, so the GCF is 6. That one example makes the claim sometimes true.
choiceFeedback: A number is a factor of itself. Try 6 and 18.
The GCF of 10 and 15 is 5, which is neither of them.
Try 6 and 18, both even, and 5 and 15, both odd — the same thing happens.
hints: Look for a pair where one number divides the other exactly.
What is the GCF of 6 and 18?
One example that breaks the claim settles it.
level3.stemEs: Afirmación: “El MCD de dos números siempre es menor que los dos.” ¿Siempre, a veces o nunca es cierto?
choicesEs: A veces — es igual al número menor siempre que ese número divida al mayor
Siempre — un factor común tiene que ser menor que lo que divide
Nunca — el MCD siempre es uno de los dos números
A veces — depende de si los números son pares
level3.explanationEs: El MCD nunca puede ser mayor que el número menor. Pero puede igualarlo, cuando el número menor divide exactamente al mayor. Comprueba 6 y 18: 6 divide a 18, así que el MCD es 6. Ese único ejemplo hace que la afirmación sea a veces verdadera.
hintsEs: Busca un par donde un número divida al otro exactamente.
¿Cuál es el MCD de 6 y 18?
Un solo ejemplo que rompa la afirmación la resuelve.

level3.stem: Two buses leave the depot together. One returns every 12 minutes, the other every 18. A student wants to know when they next leave together and answers 6. What went wrong?
choices: They found the GCF. Meeting again needs the LCM, 36 minutes
They should have added 12 + 18 to get 30 minutes
They should have multiplied 12 × 18 to get 216 minutes
level3.explanation: The student found 6, the greatest common factor of 12 and 18. A GCF answers a splitting question, not a repeating one. Meeting again needs the first shared multiple, which is the LCM. List the multiples of 12 and 18 and they first match at 36.
choiceFeedback: At 6 minutes neither bus has returned — the first is still 6 minutes away.
30 is not a multiple of 12, so the first bus is not at the depot then.
216 is a common multiple, but not the least one — they meet at 36 first.
hints: Is this a question about splitting into equal groups, or about cycles repeating?
List the multiples of 12 and of 18 and find the first they share.
GCF splits; LCM repeats.
level3.stemEs: Dos autobuses salen juntos de la terminal. Uno regresa cada 12 minutos y el otro cada 18. Un estudiante quiere saber cuándo saldrán juntos otra vez y responde 6. ¿Qué salió mal?
choicesEs: Encontró el MCD. Volver a coincidir necesita el mcm, 36 minutos
level3.explanationEs: El estudiante halló 6, el máximo común divisor de 12 y 18. Un MCD responde a una pregunta de repartir, no de repetir. Volver a coincidir necesita el primer múltiplo común, que es el mcm. Enumera los múltiplos de 12 y de 18 y coinciden por primera vez en 36.
hintsEs: ¿Es una pregunta de repartir en grupos iguales o de ciclos que se repiten?
Haz la lista de múltiplos de 12 y de 18 y busca el primero que comparten.
El MCD reparte; el mcm repite.

level3.stem: Asking for the LCM of 4 and 6, Kai lists multiples until they match: 4, 8, 12 and 6, 12. Nia multiplies 4 × 6 = 24. Whose method gives the least common multiple?
choices: Kai — 12 is the first shared multiple; Nia's 24 is a common multiple but not the least
Nia — multiplying the two numbers always gives the LCM
Both — 12 and 24 are equally correct answers
Neither — the LCM of 4 and 6 is 2
level3.explanation: Multiplying 4 × 6 always lands on a common multiple, so Nia's 24 does work. But the question asks for the least one. Kai listed the multiples and found they first match at 12. 4 and 6 share the factor 2, and multiplying counts that factor twice.
choiceFeedback: It gives a common multiple every time, but the least one only when the numbers share no factor.
Least means first. 12 comes before 24.
2 is the greatest common factor of 4 and 6, not a multiple of either.
hints: Read the question again — least common multiple.
Is 12 a multiple of both 4 and 6?
If 12 works and comes before 24, which one is least?
level3.stemEs: Al pedir el mcm de 4 y 6, Kai hace listas de múltiplos hasta que coinciden: 4, 8, 12 y 6, 12. Nia multiplica 4 × 6 = 24. ¿El método de quién da el mínimo común múltiplo?
choicesEs: El de Kai — 12 es el primer múltiplo compartido; el 24 de Nia es común pero no el mínimo
El de Nia — multiplicar los dos números siempre da el mcm
Los dos — 12 y 24 son respuestas igual de correctas
Ninguno — el mcm de 4 y 6 es 2
level3.explanationEs: Multiplicar 4 × 6 siempre cae en un múltiplo común, así que el 24 de Nia sí funciona. Pero la pregunta pide el menor. Kai enumeró los múltiplos y encontró que coinciden por primera vez en 12. 4 y 6 comparten el factor 2, y multiplicar cuenta ese factor dos veces.
hintsEs: Vuelve a leer la pregunta — mínimo común múltiplo.
¿Es 12 múltiplo de 4 y de 6?
Si 12 funciona y viene antes que 24, ¿cuál es el mínimo?
